ai-at-work.title: Vibe coding platform Base44 launches own model as AI startups seek defensibility
ai-at-work.excerpt: Wix-owned vibe coding platform Base44 has started rolling out its own AI model — with hopes that it will eventually outperform frontier models.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Base44, a Wix-owned coding platform, is building its own AI model instead of relying on third-party options like OpenAI. This matters because it signals a shift in how workplace tools are architected: companies are betting that owning their AI stack beats depending on external providers who could change pricing, access, or terms overnight. The irony is thick though, because every startup claiming AI defensibility is basically saying "our moat is that we trained on the same internet you did, but we did it in our garage."

ai-at-work.title: Anthropic and Gov. Newsom forge deal allowing California government to use Claude at half price
ai-at-work.excerpt: As Anthropic forges a closer relationship with the state of California, the federal government has made an enemy out of the OpenAI rival.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic cut a deal with California's government to provide Claude AI at a 50 percent discount, which apparently has Washington upset with the company. This matters because it shows how AI tools are becoming infrastructure decisions for large organizations, and whoever controls the pricing and access controls the adoption strategy. The real story here isn't about discounts or politics—it's that government picked Claude over ChatGPT, which means your org needs to stop assuming OpenAI wins every room and actually evaluate what tool fits your actual work.

ai-at-work.title: South Korean tech giants commit over $550B to ease ‘RAMageddon’
ai-at-work.excerpt: The world's two largest memory chip companies vow to build more memory lab fabs as South Korea positions itself as an AI tech powerhouse country.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: South Korea's Samsung and SK Hynix are dropping over $550 billion to build new memory fabrication plants, basically betting the farm that AI demand for RAM and chips won't cool down anytime soon. For those of us managing digital workplaces, this matters because it directly affects the cost and availability of the infrastructure running your collaboration tools, cloud services, and employee devices over the next five years. Honestly, watching chip companies throw half a trillion dollars at a problem is refreshing compared to the usual "we'll figure it out later" approach most enterprise IT takes.

tools-tech.title: Disappointed with AI, Ford moves to re-hire 350 former workers
tools-tech.excerpt: Ford has rehired approximately 350 experienced engineers after the company’s investment in AI and automated quality control systems failed to meet expectations, according to Bloomberg. In short, the t
tools-tech.dwp_take: Ford spent big on AI quality control systems, found they couldn't actually catch manufacturing defects, and now they're bringing back 350 experienced engineers they'd let go. This matters because it's a real-world reminder that AI doesn't replace human judgment in complex problem-solving, especially when quality and safety are on the line. After three decades watching tech solutions get oversold, I can tell you this movie has a predictable ending: turns out experienced people still know things that algorithms don't.

tools-tech.dwp_take: Italy's competition watchdog is investigating Microsoft for allegedly burying the details about Copilot integration, price hikes, and automatic plan upgrades in Microsoft 365 subscriptions. This matters because it's a real test of whether vendors can quietly slip price increases past enterprise customers or if regulators will finally hold them accountable for the fine print games. After three decades, I can tell you that Microsoft's playbook of "surprise, your subscription just got more expensive and fancier" is as old as software licensing itself, so watching a regulator actually push back is genuinely refreshing.

digital-culture.title: New data: AI makes work easier. And lonelier

digital-culture.dwp_take: A Workday study found that employees using AI report less burnout, higher productivity, and more confidence, but the headline warns that AI adoption is making workplaces lonelier. Here's the thing: you can boost productivity all day long, but a burned-out team that never talks to each other is just a quiet version of the problem you started with.

digital-culture.title: Exclusive: Inside Amazon’s brutal AI-centric app-ification of HR

digital-culture.dwp_take: Amazon is replacing human judgment in HR decisions with AI systems that workers say are arbitrary and inflexible, particularly affecting warehouse staff who face sudden terminations based on algorithmic performance metrics. This matters because it signals how far companies will push automation into people operations, potentially creating a template that other large employers might copy. The irony is thick: a company brilliant at optimizing logistics is apparently treating its own workforce like inventory to be minimized rather than people who deserve transparency about the systems judging them.

digital-culture.title: ‘Suppressed talents’: How the workplace is still failing neurodivergent workers

digital-culture.dwp_take: Companies are hiring neurodivergent workers through specialized programs, but the article suggests most aren't actually supporting them well once they're in the door. This matters because hiring someone is only half the battle; without proper workplace design, management training, and flexibility, you're just checking a diversity box while crushing the very people you recruited. The irony is thick: we've gotten good at finding neurodivergent talent, but most organizations still run offices designed for neurotypical brains, which is like buying a sports car and only driving it in parking lots.
